# Self-efficacy and Digital Technologies

### Self-efficacy and digital learning

Self-efficacy, originally formulated by @bandura_selfefficacy_1982, refers to individuals’ judgments about their capability to execute the actions required to manage prospective situations (p. 122). This construct is central to human agency, as it helps explain how people approach challenges, sustain effort in the face of setbacks, and build competence in complex domains. Self-efficacy beliefs support goal setting, persistence, and the interpretation of performance feedback, thereby shaping learning and achievement across a wide range of contexts [@bandura_selfefficacy_1995; @steele_stereotype_1995; @bandura_selfefficacy_1997].

Self-efficacy is particularly relevant for understanding learning processes involving digital technologies [@moos_learning_2009; @hatlevik_digital_2015; @aesaert_accuracy_2017]. A substantial body of research has examined how self-efficacy beliefs relate to the adoption of new technologies and the development of digital competence; however, measurement approaches remain fragmented. Early work focused on general computer self-efficacy and confidence in the use of specific software applications [@compeau_computer_1995; @durndell_computer_2002; @moos_learning_2009; @weigel_technical_2014], whereas other strands emphasized self-efficacy for internet navigation and online communication [@eastin_internet_2000a; @hsu_internet_2004; @liang_internet_2008]. This diversity of operationalizations highlights an ongoing challenge: although self-efficacy in digital environments is theoretically meaningful, it is empirically sensitive to how digital tasks are defined and grouped.

### From ICT self-efficacy to Digital Self-Efficacy (DSE)

As digital technologies became increasingly hybrid, combining computational components with networked social interaction, research converged around broader constructs such as ICT self-efficacy, which integrate internet-based tasks with more technical and computer-related activities within a single line of inquiry [@papastergiou_enhancing_2010; @aesaert_exploring_2014]. Considering this, several studies adopted a bidimensional approach that distinguishes between (a) general digital tasks related to information processing, communication, and content creation, and (b) more advanced or specialized computational tasks such as programming or web development [@aesaert_exploring_2014; @hatlevik_students_2018; @rohatgi_role_2016]. Studies adopting this framework have consistently identified contrasting associations with key variables related to competence development: self-efficacy in general digital tasks tends to align positively with broader digital proficiency, whereas self-efficacy in specialized domains often shows weaker, null, or even inverse relationships [@rohatgi_role_2016; @gebhardt_gender_2019; @aydin_multilevel_2022].

More recently, @ulfert-blank_assessing_2022 argued that traditional ICT self-efficacy instruments may struggle to keep pace with rapid technological change. Because many measures are tied to specific applications, interfaces, or devices, they can become outdated as digital systems evolve. In response, @ulfert-blank_assessing_2022 proposed the construct of digital self-efficacy (DSE), defined as individuals’ confidence in their ability to organize and execute the actions required to successfully perform digital tasks across diverse and changing contexts. This conceptualization draws on the European Digital Competence Framework (DigComp) [@europeancommissionjointresearchcentre_digcomp_2022], emphasizing that self-efficacy measures in digital environments should remain coherent across a broad range of tasks and technological ecologies. Accordingly, we adopt the label digital self-efficacy rather than ICT self-efficacy to highlight that the target of the construct is not a specific set of devices or applications.

## Operationalizations of DSE in international large-scale assessments

A major motivation for this study is that large-scale assessments operationalize digital self-efficacy in ways that differ substantially in both content and dimensionality. Such differences can influence how cross-national inequalities are interpreted and whether findings accumulate meaningfully across studies. Two prominent international large-scale assessments are ICILS and PISA, both of which include student-reported measures related to digital self-efficacy.

### ICILS and the bidimensional approach to DSE

The International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS), conducted by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement (IEA), is the primary large-scale assessment that adopts and maintains a bidimensional approach to ICT self-efficacy. ICILS assesses students’ Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) through standardized performance tests while also collecting survey data on digital-related attitudes and background variables. The study has been administered three times (2013, 2018, and 2023), using nationally representative samples of eighth-grade students across multiple educational systems.

ICILS draws on Bandura’s conceptualization of self-efficacy as perceived capability to execute courses of action [@bandura_perceived_1993] and applies it to students’ confidence in performing ICT-related tasks [@fraillon_iea_2025]. Since its inception, ICILS has distinguished between (a) self-efficacy in general ICT tasks, defined as confidence in everyday digital activities such as information retrieval, online communication, and content creation, and (b) self-efficacy in specialized ICT tasks, defined as confidence in more technically advanced activities such as programming or database management [@fraillon_iea_2025]. This distinction reflects the idea that confidence in routine digital engagement may function differently from confidence in high-level technical creation.

Although the bidimensional structure has remained stable, the composition and wording of item batteries have evolved across cycles to mirror the changing digital landscape. Between 2013 and 2018, the terminology shifted from “basic” and “advanced” to “general” and “specialized”, and items were recalibrated accordingly. The 2023 cycle introduced more substantial modifications: the specialized dimension was narrowed to focus more strongly on visual coding, text-based programming, and web creation, moving away from earlier items related to local networks or database management, while the general dimension incorporated updated items reflecting contemporary information literacy demands (e.g., identifying original sources). Item stems were also revised to reduce explicit references to “computers”, acknowledging the diversity of devices used by students.

Psychometric validation of the bidimensional ICILS self-efficacy framework has been consistently documented across cycles, although the methodological strategies have evolved. In the 2013 and 2018 cycles, dimensionality was examined using exploratory procedures in field trials and later confirmed through Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) within a Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) framework [@fraillon_icils_2015]. The 2018 cycle extended this approach by using multi-group CFA to evaluate measurement invariance across educational systems [@fraillon_iea_2020]. In the 2023 cycle, validation shifted toward an Item Response Theory (IRT) framework, using Partial Credit Models (PCM) and multi-group PCM to assess fit and cross-national comparability [@fraillon_iea_2025]. Taken together, evidence from ICILS supports the operationalization of digital self-efficacy as two related but distinct dimensions.

The empirical distinctiveness of the bidimensional framework is reinforced by the diverging relationships that general and specialized self-efficacy exhibit with digital competence and gender across diverse educational systems. Consistent analyses from ICILS international reports and independent studies demonstrate that self-efficacy in general ICT tasks functions as a robust, positive predictor of CIL achievement [@rohatgi_role_2016; @aydin_multilevel_2022; @fraillon_students_2020; @rozman_students_2025]. Conversely, self-efficacy in specialized tasks has repeatedly shown a null or even negative association with CIL performance. This discrepancy is often attributed to a “misalignment” between the high-level technical skills encompassed by specialized ICT self-efficacy (e.g., programming) and the information-management focus of CIL assessments, in which technical expertise does not necessarily translate into informational competence [@rohatgi_role_2016; @fraillon_iea_2020]. Furthermore, this distinction reveals important gender dynamics: while boys consistently report higher specialized self-efficacy, this gap disappears in the general dimension [@gebhardt_gender_2019], even though girls outperform boys in CIL scores across almost all educational systems [@kennedy_relationships_2025].

### PISA and the unidimensional approach to DSE

The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), coordinated by the OECD, evaluates 15-year-old students’ ability to apply knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics, and science to real-life challenges [@oecd_pisa_2023b]. Since its first cycle in 2000, PISA has expanded its contextual questionnaires and frameworks to capture students’ exposure to and engagement with digital technologies. The latest published cycle (PISA 2022) includes measures related to ICT use, access, and digital competence [@oecd_pisa_2023].

In PISA, self-efficacy related to digital tasks functions as an important indicator of students’ perceived capacity to perform digital activities, particularly given the absence of an ICT performance assessment comparable to ICILS. PISA’s framework aligns with DigComp by covering multiple competence areas, including information, communication, content creation, safety, and problem solving [@europeancommissionjointresearchcentre_digcomp_2022; @oecd_pisa_2023]. Consequently, the PISA digital self-efficacy battery includes items that extend beyond the ICILS operationalization, incorporating tasks such as protecting data privacy or representing computational solutions as algorithms.

Despite overlap in item scope and wording, as can be observed in @tbl-comparison, PISA differs from ICILS in its treatment of dimensionality. PISA operationalizes digital self-efficacy as a unidimensional construct, treating variation across heterogeneous tasks as reflecting a single latent continuum rather than distinct underlying dimensions [@oecd_pisa_2018_framework; @oecd_pisa_2023]. PISA’s psychometric validation relies primarily on IRT scaling, often using Partial Credit Models, supported by exploratory analyses such as principal component analyses to justify the unidimensional structure [@oecd_pisa_2024]. Scale quality is evaluated using item-fit indices, category functioning, reliability indicators, and multi-group IRT procedures to support cross-national comparability [@oecd_pisa_2024; @adams_wu_wilson_2012_conquest].

However, unlike ICILS, multidimensional alternatives for digital self-efficacy have not been systematically tested within the PISA framework, nor has it been explicitly examined whether item groupings comparable to ICILS’ general and specialized domains form empirically distinguishable latent factors. As a result, although PISA’s digital self-efficacy scale may demonstrate strong psychometric properties under a unidimensional specification, the question of whether students’ digital self-efficacy is more accurately represented by a bidimensional structure remains open and requires explicit empirical assessment.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "DSE item comparison between PISA and ICILS."

library(kableExtra)
library(openxlsx)

table <- openxlsx::read.xlsx(here::here("input", "documents", "batteries_icils_pisa_selfeff_comparison.xlsx"), fillMergedCells = TRUE)
table[is.na(table)] <- ""

table |>
  dplyr::select(Competence.area,Competence,Common.label,ICILS.Label,PISA.Label,Type.of.DSE)|>
  knitr::kable() |>
scroll_box(height="800px")
```

### Implications for cross-national and gender research

The unidimensional operationalization of digital self-efficacy has substantive consequences for how digital inequality is described and interpreted. Studies using the PISA ICT self-efficacy battery as a single latent construct consistently report significant associations with gender, socioeconomic status, ICT use, motivational orientations toward technology, and academic achievement in reading, mathematics, and science [@chen_ictrelated_2020; @yu_ict_2022; @hori_impact_2021; @kunina-habenicht_ict_2020]. These findings suggest that digital self-efficacy, as measured in PISA, functions as a meaningful predictor of educational outcomes [@yu_ict_2022]. At the same time, collapsing heterogeneous digital tasks into a single continuum implies functional equivalence between qualitatively different forms of digital engagement, ranging from routine information and communication tasks to more specialized and computationally demanding activities [@oecd_pisa_2023].

Emerging evidence suggests that the heterogeneity of digital tasks may matter. While self-efficacy related to general or information-oriented digital skills tends to show robust positive associations with achievement and background variables, self-efficacy related to more specialized or computational domains often displays weaker, null, or even reverse relationships [@tomte_genderdifferences_2011; @hristov_understanding_2026]. Yet, despite these recurrent patterns, such dimensional distinctions have rarely been subjected to formal tests of construct validity or cross-national measurement invariance, which limits confidence in substantive interpretations of gender inequalities or between-country differences.

When comparing psychological or educational constructs across social groups or countries, measurement invariance is a critical methodological requirement. Without evidence that a scale functions similarly across populations, differences in latent means or associations may reflect measurement artifacts rather than genuine disparities [@davidov_measurement_2014; @leitgob_measurement_2023]. This concern is particularly relevant for digital self-efficacy, as cross-national variation in digital experiences, institutional exposure to ICT, and cultural expectations may shape how students interpret and respond to self-efficacy items [@gebauer_crosscultural_2021; @hatlevik_students_2018; @senkbeil_ictrelated_2022]. Educational systems may attach different meanings to similar technology-related tasks due to differences in curricula, infrastructure, and the social valuation of technological skills [@martin-parraga_selfperception_2023; @annemann_teachers_2025; @conte_unlocking_2025].

While the two-dimensional structure proposed by ICILS has been widely used and supported in cross-national research [@campos_digital_2024; @gebhardt_gender_2019; @karpinski_noncognitive_2023; @rohatgi_role_2016], and some studies have applied similar item groupings to PISA data [@tomte_genderdifferences_2011; @hristov_understanding_2026], no study has systematically examined whether a comparable bidimensional digital self-efficacy construct can be established and validated across both assessments. In addition, although partial cross-national invariance has been tested for the ICILS digital self-efficacy scales [@fraillon_iea_2025; @campos_digital_2024] and gender invariance has been explored for bidimensional specifications in PISA [@hristov_understanding_2026], cross-assessment comparability remains largely unaddressed.

Building on this framework, we test the following hypotheses:

$H_{1}$: A two-dimensional model of digital self-efficacy (general and specialized) can be identified in both PISA 2022 and ICILS 2023.

$H_{2}$: The two-dimensional measurement model of digital self-efficacy is invariant across countries.

$H_{3}$: The two-dimensional measurement model of digital self-efficacy is invariant between girls and boys.

$H_{4}$: Gender differences in digital self-efficacy are dimension-specific, such that boys report higher levels of specialized digital self-efficacy than girls, whereas gender differences in general digital self-efficacy are smaller or absent.
